correlation-functions.title: Correlation Functions and Wick's Theorem
correlation-functions.content:
Probability amplitudes for a set of interacting particles to propagate between distinct spacetime coordinates form the mathematical foundation of relativistic quantum field theory. In the standard formulation of quantum electrodynamics, these vacuum expectation values, often referred to as Green's functions, represent the primary link between mathematical field operators and physical scattering experiments. For a system of fields, the n-point function measures the correlation between field fluctuations at different spacetime coordinates, written as \( G^{(n)}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \langle 0 | T\phi(x_1) \phi(x_2) \dots \phi(x_n) | 0 \rangle \). This expectation value describes how a local excitation at one point affects the field configuration at another location, defining the causal propagation of information. In the simplest case of a two-point function, the amplitude describes the propagator \( D_F(x - y) \), which measures the transition probability for a single particle to travel between two events. By translating field operators into complex amplitudes, these functions provide the mathematical framework required to analyze particle interactions.

Causal propagation of fields relies on the time-ordering operator to arrange field operator products according to their temporal coordinates. Because field operators do not commute at timelike separations, their order is critical for constructing gauge-invariant amplitudes that preserve the causal structure of spacetime. The time-ordering operator \( T \) acts by rearranging the operators such that those corresponding to later times are positioned to the left. This ordering ensures that the resulting amplitudes are consistent with the path integral formulation, where time evolution is integrated chronologically. For two scalar fields, the time-ordered product is written as \( T\phi(x)\phi(y) = \theta(x^0 - y^0)\phi(x)\phi(y) + \theta(y^0 - x^0)\phi(y)\phi(x) \), where \( \theta \) is the Heaviside step function. This mathematical definition prevents physical signals from propagating backward in time, anchoring the causal topology of the field in the temporal ordering of events.

Algebraic evaluation of these time-ordered products in free field theories is simplified by Wick's theorem, which reduces n-point functions to products of two-point functions. The theorem states that any time-ordered product of fields can be decomposed into a sum of normal-ordered terms and all possible contractions, written as \( T(\phi_1 \dots \phi_n) = :\phi_1 \dots \phi_n: + \sum \text{contractions} \). In this expansion, the contractions represent the free propagators \( D_F(x_i - x_j) \) between pairs of coordinates. By converting the time-ordered product into normal-ordered terms, the theorem allows physicists to evaluate the vacuum expectation values directly, since the normal-ordered terms vanish when acting on the vacuum state. This algebraic decomposition forms the foundation for the perturbational expansion of interacting field theories, providing the mathematical rules for constructing Feynman diagrams. Through this relation, the theorem links the algebraic properties of operators to the topological structures of scattering diagrams.

Vanishing of the normal-ordered terms when acting on the vacuum state simplifies the calculation of Green's functions to a sum over all possible pairwise contractions. Because the creation and annihilation operators within the normal-ordered fields are arranged with annihilation operators to the right, their expectation value \( \langle 0 | :\phi_1 \dots \phi_n: | 0 \rangle \) is identically zero. Consequently, the n-point correlation function of a free theory is expressed solely as the sum of all possible full contractions between pairs of fields. For a four-point function, this contraction scheme yields three distinct pairings of the four coordinates, written as \( \langle 0 | T\phi_1\phi_2\phi_3\phi_4 | 0 \rangle = D_F(12)D_F(34) + D_F(13)D_F(24) + D_F(14)D_F(23) \). Each term in this sum corresponds to a different topology of particle propagation, representing the independent pathways through which the field fluctuations can correlate. This combinatorial structure ensures that the propagation of fields is represented consistently across all coordinate separations.

Relating these unmeasurable correlation functions to physical scattering amplitudes requires the LSZ reduction formula, which projects the poles of the Green's functions onto the asymptotic states of the system. By translating the field configurations from coordinate space to momentum space \( p^\mu \), the formula connects the residues of the multi-point functions to the physical S-matrix elements \( S_{fi} \). This projection isolates the on-shell poles where the momentum satisfies the relativistic mass-shell condition \( p^2 = m^2 \), discarding the off-shell fluctuations that do not propagate to the detectors. The resulting scattering amplitudes describe the probability for particles to interact and deflect, bridging the gap between quantum field fluctuations and macroscopic detections. Through this mathematical reduction, the theory links the microscopic correlations of the vacuum to the observable cross-sections of particle physics experiments, securing the empirical foundation of quantum field theory.

position-transformation.title: Position Transformation
position-transformation.content:
Translating the coordinate descriptions of a physical event between different reference frames requires a consistent set of algebraic mapping rules. In classical mechanics, this translation is formalized by the Galilean transformation, which assumes that space is an absolute Euclidean manifold and time is an independent, universal parameter. This coordinate mapping ensures that the equations of motion are invariant for all observers moving at constant relative velocities. For two inertial frames \( S \) and \( S' \) where the latter moves at a constant velocity \( \mathbf{v} \) along the x-axis, the coordinate changes are described by linear relations. By linking the coordinate origins of different observers, the transformation guarantees that physical laws are independent of the observer's location. This relative structure establishes the foundation for classical kinematics, ensuring that the description of motion is consistent across the entire spatial domain.

The mathematical expression of this classical shift is formulated by subtracting the relative velocity of the reference frames from the spatial coordinates of the event. For a point located at coordinate \( x \) in frame \( S \), its position \( x' \) in the moving frame \( S' \) is given by the relation: \[ x' = x - vt, \quad y' = y, \quad z' = z \] where \( v \) is the relative speed and \( t \) is the coordinate time. This linear subtraction reflects the assumption that the coordinates of space scale uniformly across both reference systems. In this framework, the spatial distance between any two simultaneous events remains invariant under the transformation, allowing physicists to define rigid bodies. By translating the coordinates linearly, the mapping ensures that the acceleration of a particle is identical for all inertial observers, preserving Newton's laws of motion.

Absolute temporal progression is a fundamental assumption of this classical coordinate mapping, implying that clocks run at the same rate for all observers. This temporal invariance is expressed by the identity \( t' = t \), which establishes that the four-dimensional slices of the Block Universe are identical for all reference frames. Under this assumption, the spatial separation between two simultaneous events is a Galilean invariant quantity, meaning that the length \( L = \Delta x \) of a rigid rod is independent of the observer's state of motion. This temporal uniformity allows classical mechanics to treat space and time as completely separate structures, where space is a three-dimensional container and time flows independently. The invariance of the time coordinate ensures that the synchronization of clocks is universal, allowing for a unique cosmic time across the entire manifold.

Generalizing this coordinate transformation to include arbitrary rotations and spatial shifts leads to the full representation of the Galilean group. For a position vector \( \mathbf{r} \), the transformation is written in vector notation as: \[ \mathbf{r}' = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{v}t + \mathbf{a} \] where \( \mathbf{R} \) is a rotation matrix belonging to the special orthogonal group, \( \mathbf{v} \) is the relative velocity vector, and \( \mathbf{a} \) is a constant spatial displacement. This ten-parameter Lie group represents the complete set of symmetries that preserve the equations of motion in classical mechanics. The invariance of the Lagrangian under these transformations directly implies the conservation of momentum and energy, linking coordinate symmetries to physical invariants. By representing the transformations as group operations, the theory establishes a geometric framework for analyzing the dynamics of multi-particle systems.

Special relativity revolutionized this coordinate mapping by demonstrating that space and time are integrated into a single four-dimensional spacetime manifold. Under this relativistic framework, the Galilean relations are replaced by the Lorentz transformations, which mix the spatial and temporal coordinates to preserve the constancy of the speed of light. For a frame moving along the x-axis, the coordinates transform as: \[ x' = \gamma(x - vt), \quad t' = \gamma(t - \frac{vx}{c^2}) \] where \( \gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2} \) is the Lorentz factor and \( c \) is the speed of light. This formulation shows that simultaneous events in one frame are not simultaneous in another, violating the absolute time assumption of classical mechanics. The classical Galilean transformation is recovered as a non-relativistic limit in the regime where the relative speed is much smaller than the speed of light.

Differentiable properties of flat affine space provide the geometric origin for these coordinate mappings, where the absence of curvature ensures that coordinate lines remain straight. The vanishing connection of flat space implies that the geodesic paths of free particles are straight lines, satisfying the classical law of inertia. Position transformations are mathematically defined as the set of all affine mappings that preserve this flatness in the coordinate representation \( x^\mu \), ensuring that the metric tensor \( g_{\mu\nu} \) remains constant. By mapping straight lines to straight lines, the transformations preserve the physical state of uniform motion, anchoring our scientific realism in the geometric structure of space. Through this geometric formulation, the coordinate transformations serve as the primary tool for translating physical descriptions between different observers, securing the objectivity of physical laws.

coriolis-force.title: Coriolis Force
coriolis-force.content:
Objects in motion relative to a rotating coordinate system experience a velocity-dependent deflection that arises from the acceleration of the reference frame. In classical mechanics and meteorology, this deflection is modeled by introducing a fictitious force that acts perpendicular to the velocity of the body. This inertial interaction, known as the Coriolis Force, does not represent a physical interaction with another body, but is a geometric correction required when using a rotating frame. For a particle of mass \( m \) moving with velocity \( \mathbf{v} \) in a system rotating with angular velocity \( \boldsymbol{\omega} \), the force deflects the trajectory sideways. This deflection is critical for modeling atmospheric and oceanic circulation, where the rotation of the Earth drives the large-scale wind patterns. By modifying the equations of motion, the force accounts for the non-inertial acceleration of the coordinate system.

The mathematical characterization of this velocity-dependent deflection is formulated as the cross product of the frame's angular velocity and the particle's velocity. This relationship is written as the defining equation: \[ \mathbf{F}_c = -2m (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}) \] where \( m \) is the mass, \( \boldsymbol{\omega} \) is the angular velocity vector of the frame, and \( \mathbf{v} \) is the velocity vector of the particle. The negative sign and the factor of two are derived from the transformation of the acceleration vector between inertial and rotating coordinates. Because the force is proportional to the cross product, it is always perpendicular to both the axis of rotation and the velocity vector, meaning it only changes the direction of motion. In terrestrial coordinates, this perpendicular direction causes moving objects to deflect to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

Fluid systems on rotating planets exhibit this deflection as a primary driver of atmospheric circulation, generating the characteristic cyclonic patterns of storms. This rotational effect is crucial for Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics, where it governs the behavior of gas giants and stellar envelopes. The deflection of wind moving toward low-pressure centers creates a geostrophic balance, where the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis acceleration, which depends on the fluid velocity \( \mathbf{v} \) and the planetary angular velocity \( \boldsymbol{\omega} \). This balance leads to the formation of stable vortices and jet streams, showing that the non-inertial force plays a key role in the stability of planetary atmospheres. By linking the local fluid velocity to the global rotation rate, the equations model the complex dynamics of rotating fluid shells.

Unlike the conservative Centrifugal Force, this velocity-dependent interaction is non-conservative and performs no work on the moving body. Because the force vector \( \mathbf{F}_c \) is always orthogonal to the velocity vector \( \mathbf{v} \), the mechanical work done by the force is identically zero, satisfying the relation \( dW = \mathbf{F}_c \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{F}_c \cdot \mathbf{v} \, dt = 0 \). This workless steering is critical in orbital mechanics and potential theory, where the force stabilizes the orbits of particles around the Lagrangian points \( L_4 \) and \( L_5 \). In these regions, the balance between gravitational forces and the Coriolis deflection traps dust and asteroids in stable, non-decaying trajectories. This stability demonstrates that velocity-dependent non-conservative forces can lead to stable equilibrium points in rotating potentials.

Experimental demonstrations of this coordinate acceleration provide direct proof of the rotation of the Earth without reference to astronomical observations. The classic demonstration is the Foucault pendulum, whose plane of oscillation rotates over time at a rate that depends on the latitude \( \lambda \). The angular frequency of this rotation is given by \( \Omega = \omega \sin \lambda \), where \( \omega \) is the angular velocity of the Earth, showing that the deflection vanishes at the equator. By observing the rotation of the pendulum's swing, researchers can measure the rotation rate of their own reference frame, anchoring their scientific realism in local physical measurements. This experimental setup verifies that the apparent force is a consequence of the non-inertial frame, translating the rotation of the ground into an observable coordinate shift.

Hamiltonian formulations of mechanics represent this velocity-dependent force by introducing vector potentials that are mathematically identical to electromagnetic gauge fields. In Hamiltonian Mechanics, the momentum \( \mathbf{p} \) of a particle in a rotating frame is modified by the vector potential \( \mathbf{A} = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r} \), resulting in a Hamiltonian that is analogous to that of a charged particle in a magnetic field. The resulting equations of motion generate a force that mimics the electromagnetic Lorentz Force, where the rotation vector plays the role of the magnetic field. This mathematical symmetry unifies the description of rotating coordinates with the gauge theories of particle physics, illustrating a deep connection between spacetime geometry and gauge fields. Through this symplectic representation, the Coriolis deflection is integrated into the general framework of classical and quantum mechanics.
